lessons.title: Where India and the Rupee Fit Into Global Currency Dynamics

body.text: India is one of the few economies in this course with both an active devaluation on its own record, July 1991, and decades of absorbing other countries' currency wars as a bystander, from the 1931 sterling peg to the 2015 yuan shock. What India has almost never done is start one.

children.text: From Peg to Panic: The Road to July 1991

Through the 1970s and 1980s, the rupee was pegged, first informally to sterling as the last echo of the arrangement covered in the previous lesson, then from 1975 to a basket of currencies of India's major trading partners. The rate was tightly administered rather than market-determined, and a decade of import-substitution industrialisation, fiscal deficits and rising oil bills left the rupee persistently overvalued at its official rate. By early 1991, an oil price spike from the Gulf War, a widening current account deficit and a loss of investor confidence had pushed India's forex reserves down to barely a few weeks of import cover.

Unlike the passive devaluation the rupee experienced in 1931 by simply riding sterling down, this time India made an explicit, active choice. As part of the reforms attached to an IMF-backed rescue, the RBI devalued the rupee in two steps within three days.

events.title: First devaluation
events.description: The RBI devalues the rupee against a basket of major currencies by roughly 9%, its first major devaluation since 1966.

events.title: Second devaluation
events.description: A further devaluation of roughly 11% is announced just two days later, for a cumulative fall of close to 19% from the pre-1 July level.

events.title: LERMS introduced
events.description: The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System splits the exchange rate into an official rate for a portion of transactions and a market-determined rate for the rest, a transitional dual-rate system.

events.title: Rates unified
events.description: India moves to a single, market-determined exchange rate and current account convertibility, ending the dual-rate arrangement and starting the managed float regime the RBI still runs today.

body.title: Compound the Two Steps
body.prompt: The RBI devalued the rupee by roughly 9% on 1 July 1991, then a further roughly 11% on 3 July 1991, with the second cut applied to the already-devalued rate. Approximately what was the cumulative devaluation from the pre-1 July level? Use: cumulative = 1 minus [(1 minus 9%) times (1 minus 11%)], as a percentage.
body.explanation: 1 − (0.91 × 0.89) = 1 − 0.8099 = 0.1901, or about 19%. Two devaluations in three days compound rather than simply add, which is why 9% plus 11% doesn't quite get you to the commonly cited 'about 18 to 19%' figure by pure addition either, they land in the same place by coincidence of rounding, but the correct method is multiplicative.

body.text: Compare this to the 1931 rupee move from Lesson 2. In 1931, the rupee fell because sterling fell and the peg carried India along automatically, no domestic policy decision was required. In 1991, the RBI itself chose the number, twice, in the space of three days. Same currency, same direction, completely different mechanism, and only one of the two counts as India actively devaluing.

markDefs.definition: The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System, introduced in 1992, under which a portion of foreign exchange transactions settled at the official RBI rate and the rest at a market-determined rate, a transitional step toward full unification.

children.text: The two-step devaluation bought time and restored some competitiveness, but it was still an administered rate.

in 1992 was the bridge: exporters could sell 40% of their foreign exchange earnings at the less favourable official rate and 60% at the market rate, gradually shifting price discovery toward the market before the two rates merged completely in March 1993. From that point on, the rupee has floated, managed rather than fixed, which is the regime described in Lesson 1.

body.caption: India's Exchange Rate Regimes Over Time

cells: Administered rate, no independent RBI monetary policy discretion on the exchange rate
Tightly controlled, rate persistently overvalued relative to fundamentals
RBI sets a new, explicit rate twice within three days as a crisis response
Partial market pricing (60%), partial official rate (40%), a transition mechanism
Market-determined rate, RBI intervenes to smooth volatility, not to target a level

body.title: Quick Check: 1931 vs 1991
body.question: Both the 1931 and the 1991 rupee moves resulted in a weaker currency. What is the key mechanism difference between them?
options: The 1931 move was larger in percentage terms than the 1991 move
The 1931 move happened because sterling fell and the rupee's peg carried it down automatically; the 1991 move was an explicit RBI policy decision made twice within three days
The 1991 move was passive, inherited through a peg, while the 1931 move was an active RBI decision
There is no real difference, both were competitive devaluations aimed at trading partners
body.explanation: 1931 is the passive case from Lesson 2: no Indian monetary authority existed yet to make an active choice, the rupee simply followed sterling off gold. 1991 is the active case: the RBI, now decades into independent operation, chose the exact devaluation twice, as a deliberate crisis response tied to an IMF program, not to gain a competitive edge over any specific trading partner.

children.text: Has India Ever Actually Fought a Currency War?

Unlike China, India has rarely if ever been accused by trading partners of deliberately holding the rupee weak for export advantage. The RBI's own stated mandate since 1993 has been to curb excessive volatility, not to defend or push toward a specific level, and India's large forex reserve buildup since the 1990s has functioned as defensive insurance against another 1991-style crisis rather than as ammunition to hold the rupee down.

body.text: There is a structural reason India rarely plays offense on the rupee. India runs a large import bill dominated by crude oil and gold, both priced in dollars. A persistently weak rupee makes those imports costlier and feeds straight into domestic inflation. For an economy this import-dependent, chasing export competitiveness through a deliberately weak currency risks doing more damage at home than it gains abroad, which is exactly the transfer problem raised in Lesson 1.

children.text: India as Bystander: Absorbing Everyone Else's Currency Wars

The two case studies already covered in this chapter both hit India from the outside. In 2009 to 2011, Fed-driven carry trade capital pushed the rupee up along with the Brazilian real, part of the same wave Lesson 3 described, before reversing sharply as conditions changed later in the decade. In August 2015, a reference-rate decision in Beijing wiped a meaningful chunk off the Nifty within two weeks, with nothing in India's own fundamentals having changed, exactly the transmission mechanism from Lesson 1. India did not choose either episode. It managed the consequences of both.

body.title: China vs India: Two Different Relationships With Currency Wars

columns.label: China
points: Tightly managed peg or managed float, historically accused of undervaluation
Reserves and policy have at times been used to influence the yuan's level, not just its volatility
A major, deliberate participant whose moves other countries actively watch and respond to
Export competitiveness has long been an explicit strategic priority

columns.label: India
points: Managed float since 1993, RBI targets volatility, not a level
Reserves function mainly as crisis insurance, built after the 1991 near-default
Largely a rate-taker in global currency war episodes, reacting rather than initiating

body.title: Name the Regime
body.textWithBlank: Since March 1993, the rupee has operated under a ___ float, where the RBI intervenes to smooth volatility rather than to defend or target a specific exchange rate level.
body.explanation: Managed float. This is the regime referenced throughout Chapter 1, and Chapter 2 goes into exactly how the RBI defends it in practice, through intervention, reserves and the tools available to it.

cards.definition: The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System, India's 1992 dual-rate transition mechanism ahead of full rate unification in 1993.
India's two-step, active rupee devaluation of roughly 9% and 11%, a cumulative fall of about 19%, made as part of IMF-backed crisis reforms.
India's exchange rate regime since March 1993, where the rupee is market-determined but the RBI intervenes to limit excessive volatility, not to target a level.
Active: a domestic authority explicitly chooses a new rate, as India did in 1991. Passive: the currency moves automatically because it is pegged to one that moved, as India's rupee did in 1931.

points: India actively devalued the rupee by a cumulative ~19% in two steps on 1 and 3 July 1991, as part of an IMF-backed crisis response, a genuinely deliberate devaluation unlike the passive 1931 move.
LERMS in 1992 and full rate unification in March 1993 moved India permanently to a managed float, the regime referenced throughout this chapter.
India has rarely, if ever, been accused of running a currency war of its own, unlike China, largely because a large oil and gold import bill makes a persistently weak rupee costly at home.
India's post-1991 forex reserve buildup functions as crisis insurance, not as ammunition for holding the rupee down to chase export competitiveness.
Across the episodes covered in this chapter, from 1931 to 2010 to 2015, India has mostly been on the receiving end of other economies' currency decisions rather than the source of them.
This bystander position is exactly why the mechanics of RBI intervention and defence, covered next in Chapter 2, matter so much to Indian markets.

The July 1991 devaluation percentages are widely cited approximations; verify exact figures against RBI historical records before citing them elsewhere. The current forex reserves figure is deliberately left general, check the RBI's latest weekly statistical supplement for the up-to-date number rather than relying on any figure quoted here.
